THESIS STATEMENT
Fig. 1.1 Conceptual Collage: Sensory Extension
How can sensory substitution techniques used in neuroprosthetics and cognitive psychology
be translated into spatial and other design strategies to achieve an inclusive interior
which transforms, extends, and augments perceptual capacities to increase wellness and
productivity.
Thesis Design Problem: Thesis Statement 06

THESIS ABSTRACT
Studies show that about 466 million people, worldwide, are hearing
impaired and about 36 million people are legally blind (Fig. 1.2). According
to an American study from 2016, 94% of people between the ages of 57 and
85 have some kind of sensory disability, and a majority of them actually
suffer from impairments to at least two of their five main senses. With the
continuing increase in the average human life expectancy, these numbers
are expected to exponentially climb; the World Health Organization (WHO)
predicts that the number of people with hearing related disabilities will
double by the year 2050.1
Because the majority of people rely primarily on their vision to aid in spatial
cognition, spaces specifically designed for those with impaired senses
usually address the needs of the blind. Those who are exclusively hearing
impaired rarely receive specific accommodations in the world of inclusive
design. The proposed interior design addresses the spatial obstacles found
in the workplace that are specific to the deaf and the hearing-impaired
Fig. 1.2 Disabled People in the World in 2019: Facts and Figures community. It does this by implementing strategies to adapt the interior to

encourage communication and to promote workplace inclusion. In addition
to addressing the perspective of the hearing-impaired, the proposed interior
should also improve the experience of all other users in the space.

Research Framework
Worldwide, studies show that the prevalence of sensory impairments
is significantly greater compared to the number of people with
classified physical or intellectual disabilities.1,2 However, when it
comes to inclusive design, there is a much higher focus on designing
for people with physical disabilities.3 Of the two most common types
of sensory disabilities, blindness and deafness, the deaf community
tends to be at a greater disadvantage when it comes to social and
spatial recognition, acceptance, and accommodations for their
disability.4

Thesis Design Problem: Thesis Research Statement 10

Neuroprosthetic devices can be used to substitute for or aid motor, sensory, and/
or cognitive functions that have been impaired. They can be effective in, on, and
outside of the body.6 (Fig. 1.5) The first and now most common neuroprosthetic
aid used to improve hearing is the cochlear implant.7
In addition to the use of neuroprosthetics, there are alternative sensory substitution
techniques. Sensory substitution techniques are perceptual and cognitive strategies
used to circumvent one sense by translating the same information into a form that
can be understood by an alternate sense. This technique progressively advances
cognitive capacities with respect to multi-sensory perception, attention, mental
imagery, and brain plasticity. "Sensory substitution techniques provide a novel
opportunity to dissociate the stimulus, the task and the sensory modality, and thus
offer a unique way to explore the level of representation that is most crucial for
cognition."8
The design principles and function of neuroprosthetics and sensory substitution
techniques are the starting point for my interior investigation, which seeks to
transform both into a spatial and material design language that improves the
experience for the deaf.
